We live with tinnitus; we\'re not doctors. Brume draws on published research and clinical guidance we\'ve read, to offer some calm to anyone who wants to relax. It isn\'t a treatment or a medical device, and it doesn\'t replace a doctor, an ENT or an audiologist.
Everything stays on this phone. Brume has no internet access, no account and no cloud backup. Data leaves only in a file you save yourself, or in the folder you choose to sync with.

A sound the brain keeps up

Tinnitus is a sound heard with no outside source. It is very common and often goes with some hearing loss, even mild. How much it bothers you often depends less on its loudness than on the attention it pulls and the feelings it stirs.

The sound is real: you really hear it. What can change is how much room it takes. Like a ticking clock you stop noticing, the brain can learn to file it in the background; this is called habituation. Worry and focused attention slow it down, and both can be worked on.
CBT is the one approach every guideline recommends. It doesn\'t aim at the sound itself but at the weight it puts on life: sleep, mood, focus. It exists online, in groups or with a psychologist.
Hearing aids, if there\'s hearing loss

If your hearing has dropped, hearing aids bring the world\'s sounds back, so the tinnitus is less alone in the foreground. Without hearing loss they haven\'t shown a benefit. A hearing test is the first step.
A soft sound (rain, a fan, pink noise) often makes tinnitus stand out less, and many people find it calming. Trials haven\'t shown one device or sound beating another. It\'s real comfort, not a fix.
Set the sound just under your tinnitus so the two blend.

Giving up coffee doesn\'t change tinnitus, according to a double-blind placebo-controlled trial: caffeinated and decaf days came out the same, and withdrawal mostly brought headaches. A large cohort even found fewer new cases among the heaviest coffee drinkers; that\'s an association, not proof of an effect.
Keep your intake steady; the “coffee” tag in the Journal lets you see how it goes for you.
Studies don\'t make alcohol a cause of tinnitus; some even link moderate drinking to fewer cases, which shows nothing either way. Some people notice louder tinnitus the next day, others nothing.
The “alcohol” tag, to notice without jumping to conclusions.
Smoking is linked to slightly more tinnitus in several studies, mostly cross-sectional; cohort studies don\'t all confirm it. Stopping is good for your health generally, ears included.
Cutting salt has no shown benefit for ordinary tinnitus. It\'s advised for Ménière\'s disease (vertigo, a full ear, fluctuating hearing), and even there trials are lacking.

Tinnitus often feels more intrusive in stressful times, an “emotional barometer”. Stress didn\'t create it, but it changes how much attention it gets. Relaxation and mindfulness help many people live with it.
The “stress” tag, and a few minutes of slow breathing with a soft sound.
More active people report a bit less bother, but these studies show links, not causes. During exercise some hear their tinnitus louder, others quieter. Moving is still good for sleep and mood.

Ginkgo and zinc do no better than placebo, and guidelines advise against them. Magnesium alone has no convincing published trial. Melatonin may help some people sleep, but any effect on tinnitus itself is uncertain.
Ask a doctor or pharmacist before any supplement.

Some medicines can bring on or worsen tinnitus, often only for a while. If in doubt, talk to the doctor who prescribed them: they can adjust the dose or suggest another. Never stop a medicine on your own.
For some people, tinnitus changes when they clench their teeth or turn their head: this is called somatic tinnitus. If that\'s you, a dentist, physio or ENT can look at your jaw or neck.
A plug of earwax can bring on tinnitus or make it louder. Wax usually works its way out; cotton buds push it deeper. A few drops of oil for a few days, or a doctor if it lasts.
Tinnitus is louder in the evening quiet, worry keeps you awake, and poor sleep makes tinnitus weigh more. CBT for insomnia has done well in people with tinnitus, for sleep and for distress.
Go to bed when sleepy, keep the bed for sleep, get up if you lie awake long.
A soft sound in the bedroom (a fan, rain) is common advice; many people sleep better without total silence. Keep it low, use a timer, and prefer the speaker to earbuds.

Decibels (dB) measure how strong a sound is, on a scale that doesn\'t climb in a straight line. +3 dB is twice the energy; +10 dB sounds about twice as loud. So 90 dB isn\'t “a bit more” than 80: it\'s ten times the energy.

Rough figures, which vary by source: conversation 50–65 dB; busy street 70–80; hairdryer or metro 80–95; headphones at max about 100–105; concert or club 100–110. Hearing risk starts around 85 dB over time; pain around 120. In France, music venues are capped at 102 dB(A) averaged over 15 minutes.
Time counts as much as volume
WHO sets a weekly benchmark: 80 dB for 40 hours. Every +3 dB halves the time: 83 dB, 20 h; 86 dB, 10 h; 89 dB, about 5 h. At concert level, a week\'s dose goes in minutes.
Brume shows your listening time in the Journal.

A sound-meter app gives an idea, not an exact reading. On iPhone, NIOSH\'s free app stayed within ±2 dB in the lab; Android apps varied widely between phones in NIOSH\'s tests. Android can also track headphone “sound dose” over a rolling 7 days and warn at 100%, depending on the maker.

Three kinds. Foam: cheap, very effective when inserted well, but it muffles the highs. Reusable silicone: handy, fit varies. Custom-moulded, made by an audiologist: comfortable, long-lasting, often with a filter.
For foam, roll it, pull your ear up and back, hold for a few seconds.
SNR (NRR in the US) is measured in the lab, with a perfect fit. Real life often gives much less; OSHA suggests counting about half the NRR. A well-fitted 20 dB plug beats a badly fitted 35 dB one.

Filtered plugs lower all frequencies about equally: music and voices stay natural, just quieter. Handy at concerts, rehearsals or in bars. Not every “flat” plug is flat: a measured attenuation curve beats a promise on the box.
Concerts, clubs, festivals, power tools, the lawnmower, the motorbike, fireworks, a loud gym class: yes. If you have to shout to someone a metre away, it\'s probably over 85 dB.

In everyday life, earplugs all the time do more harm than good: deprived of sound, the ear “turns up the gain”, tinnitus stands out and ordinary sounds can start to hurt (hyperacusis). Total silence does the same. Earplugs are for loud noise; the rest of the time, a soft background.

See a doctor today if your hearing dropped suddenly (within three days, in the last month), if strong vertigo comes with the tinnitus, if it started after a blow to the head, or if your face feels weak or numb.
Book an appointment if the tinnitus beats with your heart, if it\'s in one ear and new or getting worse, or if your hearing drops over a few weeks.
If tinnitus has weighed on your mood or sleep for weeks, a doctor can refer you to CBT or a specialist team. If it ever feels like too much, the lines below are there for that.

Tinnitus can\'t be seen, which makes it hard to understand. A simple line often does: “I hear a sound all the time; some days it takes more room.” Saying what helps (some background sound, a quiet break) works better than describing the sound.
Associations offer listening lines and support groups, families included. Many people find that talking with others who live with it changes how they relate to it.
Short cards on what research says, each with how well it\'s supported.
Studies on tone patterns like this one are few and small: try it if you\'re curious, and stop if it doesn\'t suit you.

If a sound catches you, the one in your ears perhaps, you can notice it without trying to change it. Gently come back to the sounds around you, to your breath. No need to check whether the sound is still there.
